items.label: section_header
items.text: TO MAKE BARIUM SULFATE

items.label: section_header
items.text: EXTENSION WORK

items.label: text
items.text: The ionic equation is:

items.label: text
items.text: Ba²+(aq) + SO4²-(aq) → BaSO4(s)

items.label: text
items.text: Safety Note: Wear eye protection. The lead nitrate and sulfate are toxic and all skin contact must be avoided.

items.label: section_header
items.text: WHAT DO WE MIX TOGETHER TO MAKE INSOLUBLE SALTS?

items.label: text
items.text: Our procedure for making insoluble salts is to mix together two solutions containing soluble salts, but how do we know what to mix together? To determine this, two really useful facts are:

items.label: list_item
items.text: all nitrates are soluble

items.label: list_item
items.text: all sodium and potassium salts are soluble.

items.label: text
items.text: So all we have to do is mix the nitrate of the metal part of our insoluble salt with the sodium or potassium salt of the non-metal part.

items.label: text
items.text: For instance, if we have to make lead(Il) iodide:

items.label: list_item
items.text: the metal part is lead, so we use a solution of lead(ll) nitrate

items.label: list_item
items.text: the non-metal part is iodide, so we use a solution of sodium iodide.

items.label: text
items.text: The equation for the reaction is:

items.label: text
items.text: Pb(NO3)2(aq) + 2Nal(aq)→ Pbl2(s) + 2NaNO₃(aq)

items.label: text
items.text: Figure 17.12 shows the yellow precipitate of lead(Il) iodide.

items.label: text
items.text: We can use barium nitrate solution and potassium sulfate solution:

items.label: text
items.text: Ba(NO3)₂(aq) + K_2SO4(aq) → BaSO4(s) + 2KNO3(aq)

items.label: text
items.text: The barium sulfate is a white precipitate.

items.label: text
items.text: There are other ways we could make barium sulfate. We could also use barium chloride, which is soluble in water. The sulfate part doesn't necessarily have to come from a salt; dilute sulfuric acid contains sulfate ions, so we can use that as well.

items.label: section_header
items.text: ACTIVITY 6

items.label: section_header
items.text: PRACTICAL: PREPARING A PURE, DRY SAMPLE OF LEAD(II) SULFATE

items.label: text
items.text: The following procedure is used:

items.label: list_item
items.text: Take 25 cm³ of a solution of lead(Il) nitrate in a beaker and add 25 cm³ of a solution of sodium sulfate. The amounts don't really matter as we will get rid of any excess later.

items.label: list_item
items.text: A white precipitate of lead(Il) sulfate will form.

items.label: list_item
items.text: The equation for the reaction is:

items.label: text
items.text: Pb(NO3)2(aq) + Na2SO4(aq) → PbSO4(s)+ 2NaNO3(aq)

items.label: list_item
items.text: The reaction mixture is filtered.

items.label: list_item
items.text: A white residue of lead(Ill) sulfate is left in the filter paper and a colourless solution of sodium nitrate and any excess reactants (either lead(Il) nitrate or sodium sulfate) passes through into the beaker or conical flask. The white residue on the filter paper is the compound we want, but it is contaminated with solutions of sodium nitrate and the reactant that was in excess.
